opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think we're in an interesting phase. For a while, roughly 2012 to 2020, architecture was where much of the action was: AlexNet, VGG, ResNet, DenseNet, then attention and the Transformer, then Vision Transformers. Each step felt like a big leap, and a new block design could buy you several points on ImageNet.

Since then things have consolidated a lot. The Transformer has become the default almost everywhere: language, vision, speech, multimodal models, even parts of robotics and science. Much of the field's energy has moved toward data, scale, training recipes, and post-training. In many settings, if you hold compute and data fixed and carefully tune things, a lot of architectures land surprisingly close to each other. That was part of the motivation behind ConvNeXt. We wanted to see how much of the ViT advantage came from attention itself, and how much came from the modernized training recipe and design choices around it. It turned out a pure ConvNet, modernized step by step, could match it quite well.

So my view is that architecture research hasn't died, but its role has changed. It's less about inventing a radically new block that wins a benchmark. It's more about understanding which components actually matter, simplifying, and making things more efficient and scalable. Our work on removing normalization layers, replacing LayerNorm with something as simple as a scaled tanh, is in that spirit. It asks which parts we thought were essential are really just habits.

There are still real open questions where architecture could matter a lot: long-context efficiency, state-space and hybrid models, memory, and how to build models that reason or adapt at test time more effectively. But I'd encourage people to be rigorous: control for training recipes and compute, because many claimed architectural gains disappear once you do. The most valuable contributions now are often the ones that tell us what we don't need.

r001.rationale: The response says architecture research has shifted toward data, scale, training, and efficiency, but it does not attribute reduced academic activity to academics being unable to afford the compute needed to demonstrate architectural effects at convincing scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Ravid. I'd say architecture research is in an interesting, slightly paradoxical place right now. On one hand, if you look at what people actually deploy, the field has converged dramatically. Almost everything is a Transformer, and the variations between them are honestly pretty small. So there's a narrative that architecture research is "done," that it's all about data and scale now, and that you should just stop tinkering with the model.

I don't fully buy that, for a couple of reasons. First, when we did ConvNeXt, the whole point was to ask whether the Transformer's success was really about attention, or whether it was about the training recipe and a bunch of design choices that had accumulated around it. And it turned out that if you modernize a ConvNet with those same choices, you close most of the gap. That told me the field sometimes attributes gains to the wrong component. The architecture question hasn't been settled so much as it's been bundled together with everything else, and nobody has carefully unbundled it.

Second, scale changes what matters. A lot of architectural ideas that looked important at small scale wash out when you train longer or with more data, and some that looked irrelevant become important for efficiency reasons at large scale. So I think the useful version of architecture research today is less about inventing a new block that gives you half a point on ImageNet, and more about understanding which inductive biases survive scaling and which ones don't, and about the systems side, things like how the architecture interacts with memory, hardware, and inference cost. State space models, mixture of experts, long-context attention variants, those are all really architecture questions, they just look different from the classic "new backbone" paper.

The thing I'd push back on in the community is the incentive structure. It's very easy to publish a paper where you change something, get a slightly better number, and declare a new architecture. It's much harder, and much more valuable, to do the controlled study that tells you why. I think we need more of the second kind of work, because that's what actually builds understanding rather than just a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses how scale affects architectural findings, but does not attribute reduced academic research activity to academics being unable to afford compute for convincing large-scale demonstrations.

astra-6.text:
I think architecture research is in an interesting place. A lot of attention has shifted toward data, scale, and training, and that makes sense—those things have a huge effect on performance. But I don’t think that means architecture is solved. It’s more that the questions we ask need to change.

Instead of asking whether a new component improves accuracy on one benchmark, we should ask what it buys us under a realistic compute budget. Does it make training more efficient? Does it reduce the cost of inference? Does it work across different scales and tasks? And could we get the same improvement by training a simpler model more carefully?

For me, that last question is especially interesting. Understanding why a simple architecture works well can be just as valuable as inventing something more complicated. So I’m optimistic about architecture research, but I think strong baselines and careful comparisons are increasingly important.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating architectures under realistic compute budgets, but does not attribute reduced academic research activity to academics lacking the compute needed to demonstrate effects at convincing scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think architecture research is in an interesting place. A lot of attention has shifted toward data, scale, and training, and sometimes that creates the impression that architecture is a solved problem. I don’t think it is. But the way we evaluate architectural ideas has to evolve.

An architecture doesn’t work in isolation. Its performance depends on the training recipe, the compute budget, and the hardware. If you compare a new model with an older model using a weaker training recipe, it’s hard to know where the improvement actually comes from. So I think strong, carefully controlled baselines are especially important.

There’s also a lot of room to make models simpler and more efficient. A change that looks small in terms of accuracy can be very meaningful if it makes a model faster or easier to scale. For me, the interesting question is which architectural choices really matter, under what conditions, and why.

r001.rationale: The response says architectural performance depends on the compute budget, but does not attribute reduced academic research activity to academics being unable to afford enough compute to demonstrate effects convincingly.
